title: Website Launch
content: Welcome to the official GF PriceChecker website! We're building an iOS app to help Canadians track gluten-free product price differentials for tax deductions. Stay tuned for updates on our development progress.

title: Public Beta Now Available
content:
GF PriceChecker has reached an important milestone: the public beta is now live on TestFlight.

The app provides tools for product comparison, receipt verification, and exportable expense records—all while maintaining complete data privacy through local-only storage.

Beta testing is a critical phase where real-world usage reveals opportunities for improvement that isolated development cannot uncover. Your participation helps ensure the app meets the practical needs of the celiac community.

To join the beta program, visit the Beta Testing page for complete instructions and access to the TestFlight link.

We welcome your feedback. TestFlight includes built-in feedback tools that allow you to report issues, suggest improvements, or share observations directly with the development team. Your input during this phase will directly shape the final release.

Thank you for your interest in GF PriceChecker and your willingness to contribute to a tool designed for our community.

title: Unit Pricing Is Now the Number That Counts
content:
Several months of beta feedback have reshaped how the app measures the gluten-free premium, and build 8 is now on TestFlight.

The headline change: unit price is the figure the app leads with everywhere. Not what the package cost—what it cost per hundred grams. Gluten-free products don't only cost more, they frequently contain less, and comparing sticker prices hides that. A $7.99 gluten-free loaf at 400g beside a $3.99 regular loaf at 675g looks like a $4.00 difference. Measured per gram and scaled back to the size you actually bought, the real premium is $5.63. That size-adjusted number now leads the product list, the summary dashboard, the PDF report, and the CSV export. The plain package difference is still there, labelled and kept for reference.

Capturing a product is simpler too. After scanning a shelf tag, the review screen used to hand you off to a second form partway through. It's now one continuous screen with three plain steps—name, then price, then size—and your scan results stay in front of you the whole time. Size is optional: skip it when you're in a hurry, and the app tells you which items sat out of the unit price totals rather than quietly folding them in.

Also in this build: deleting a product pair now removes its photographs instead of leaving them on the device, and a bug that dropped size data when restoring a backup has been fixed. Backup files from build 7 and earlier still import cleanly—those records simply have no size data to restore.

One piece of news from outside the app. Celiac Canada's petition for a flat refundable credit, signed by 33,000 Canadians, was declined by the government in March. The Medical Expense Tax Credit stays as it is, and itemized receipts remain your responsibility to keep. Celiac Canada is continuing to press the case. Until something changes, this app still has a job to do.

title: Budget 2026 Proposes a Flat $1,000 Celiac Claim, and GF PriceChecker Development Ends
content:
On November 5, the federal government tabled Budget 2026. It includes the change this community has been asking for: individuals with celiac disease would be able to claim an optional flat $1,000 under the Medical Expense Tax Credit for incremental gluten-free food expenses, starting with the 2026 tax year—without calculating the extra cost, and without keeping receipts for it.

A few details from the budget's tax measures are worth knowing. The flat amount is optional: each year you could claim it or itemize your actual costs instead, but not both. The existing eligibility conditions would continue to apply, and Celiac Canada notes that a medical practitioner's certification of celiac disease is still required. If more than one person claims for the same individual, the flat amount would not be available, and each would need to itemize. And it is a claim within the existing, non-refundable credit, not the $1,000 refundable credit that Celiac Canada and Petition e-6853 asked for. The credit still applies only to medical expenses above a threshold of roughly three percent of net income.

This is a proposal. It becomes law only once Parliament passes it, and the Canada Revenue Agency has not yet published guidance on how it would be claimed. Celiac Canada has welcomed the measure; its statement is on celiac.ca.

GF PriceChecker was built to handle the record-keeping the current rules demand: two shelf tags, two sizes, a receipt and a calculation for every product, all year. A flat claim with no receipts takes that work away for many people, which is the outcome this site has said all along it hoped for. So the app is no longer in development. It will not be released on the App Store or Google Play, and the public TestFlight beta is closed to new testers.

The source code is open source, at github.com/CuWilliams/GFPriceChecker. If you see a need it could still meet—a household whose costs run well above $1,000 and who would rather itemize, for example—you're welcome to build on it.

If you're already testing the app: export a backup from Settings, and your PDF or CSV records from the Reports tab, and keep them somewhere safe. TestFlight builds expire, and once the last one does, the app will no longer open. Your data has only ever lived on your device, so an export is the only other copy.

Thank you to every tester who used the app and told us what was wrong with it, and to Celiac Canada for the years of advocacy that made this change happen.
